# White Papers and References {#sec-white-papers}



A white paper is the one output that leaves the building and has to stand on its own. A
client's analyst, an investor's technical adviser or a sceptical researcher will read it
without you in the room, and will check it: whether the method is stated, whether the numbers
in the text match the tables, whether the references exist and say what the paper claims they
say. For a start-up, a benchmark or evaluation white paper is often the most credible thing it
can publish, and the most damaging if one of those checks fails.

::: opener
- Name the parts of a technical white paper and the Quarto feature behind each: numbered
  sections, cross-references, citations, a citation style and a template.
- Ask for a paper whose every figure, table and equation is referred to by number, and check
  that each reference resolves in every format.
- Cite only what you have opened, in one citation style across HTML, Word and PDF, and check
  every DOI with a script.
- Give the PDF a house template, and know when to use a journal's instead.

Start from
: your `acme-eval` repository at the end of @sec-sites, or `checkpoints/17-eval-site/`.

You build
: `whitepaper.qmd` in PDF, Word and HTML, with `references.bib`, a citation style, a reference
  checker and a house template.

Checkpoint
: `checkpoints/18-eval-whitepaper/`
:::

## What a white paper is made of {#sec-wp-vocab}

Ask for each part of the paper by its name in Quarto:

| Part | Quarto calls it |
|---|---|
| numbered sections | `number-sections: true`; `## Data {#sec-data}` |
| an equation, cited | `$$ … $$ {#eq-auc}`, then `@eq-auc` |
| a table or figure, cited | a `tbl-…` or `fig-…` label, then `@tbl-…` |
| citations | `[@key]`, from `references.bib` |
| a citation style | `csl:` and a style file; `citeproc: true` for the PDF |

: A white paper's parts, and their names in Quarto 1.10.20. {#tbl-wp-vocab}

## The paper {#sec-wp-paper}

The first prompt asks for the whole paper, from `outputs/` only: six numbered sections, ROC
AUC as a numbered equation, a table and a figure, each cited, and the guards. The second puts
it on the site.

::: {.prompt .long}
```default
Create whitepaper.qmd, a white paper for clients and investors, from outputs/ only: numbered sections (Introduction, Data, Method, Results, Limitations, Conclusion), the abstract in the body, ROC AUC as a numbered equation, a results table and the ROC figure, each cited with @eq-, @tbl- and @fig-, `fig-format: svg` for the PDF, and guards where wording depends on the results. Render it to html, typst and docx (the existing reference-doc) and check that no cross-reference shows "??".
```
:::

::: {.agent}
writes `whitepaper.qmd` · `uv run quarto render whitepaper.qmd`
:::

::: {.prompt}
```default
Add whitepaper.qmd to the site's render list and to the home page's listing, with a description. Render the site and list its pages.
```
:::

::: {.agent}
edits `_quarto.yml` and `index.qmd` · `uv run quarto render`
:::

Check it as its outside reader would. **References resolve**: search each output for "??".
**The equation is real**: in the Word file, it is an equation, not a picture of one.
**Figures are vectors**: in the PDF, zoom in on a figure's labels; they stay sharp. **Numbers
agree**: a number in the Results text equals the same number in the table. **The abstract
stands alone**: someone who reads only the abstract knows what was evaluated, the headline
result and its main limit.

The finished paper, which also numbers recall and the interval, refers to
three equations,
one table, two figures
and four sections by number. A reference that does not resolve
renders as "??", so a search of each format for it is the check a reader would make by eye,
done once: in the finished paper's three formats, it found none.

## References a reader can check {#sec-wp-refs}

A reference list is a set of claims: this work exists, and it says what we say it says. An
agent can produce a plausible reference that does not exist (@sec-water-dashboard), so the
prompt requires opening each one, and allows only what was confirmed. A DOI's record lives
with its registry: *Crossref* for most journal articles, *DataCite* for most datasets, each
with a free API:

::: {.prompt .long}
```default
Cite the dataset, Moro et al. (2014), Mitchell et al. (2019), and the papers behind ROC analysis, the bootstrap and calibration, from references.bib. Look each DOI up with the Crossref API, or DataCite's for the dataset, open it, and add only entries whose authors, title and year you could confirm. Download apa.csl from the official CSL styles repository, use it with `citeproc: true` for typst, render all three formats and check that their reference lists match.
```
:::

::: {.agent}
queries Crossref · edits `references.bib` · downloads `csl/apa.csl` · renders three formats
:::

The project's `references.bib`, which the paper shares with the model card, holds
seven works, all of them cited by the paper. All but one have
a DOI in the file; the statute, which has none, was confirmed at legislation.gov.uk:

| Key | Year | Cited by |
|---|---|---|
| `moro2014bank` | 2014 | paper, card |
| `moro2014datadriven` | 2014 | paper, card |
| `mitchell2019modelcards` | 2019 | paper, card |
| `equalityact2010s4` | 2010 | paper, card |
| `fawcett2006roc` | 2006 | paper |
| `efron1979bootstrap` | 1979 | paper |
| `niculescumizil2005calibration` | 2005 | paper |

: The project's references, from the finished `references.bib`, and the documents that cite each. {#tbl-wp-refs}


A citation style is a file. The Citation Style Language's official repository holds thousands,
APA and IEEE among them, and most journals', each under a Creative Commons licence; download
the one your readers expect and name it in `csl:`, in a site's `_quarto.yml` so that every
document on the site cites alike, as the finished project does. A reference manager such as
Zotero exports the same `.bib` format.

| What you see | The fix |
|---|---|
| A second "Bibliography" heading in the PDF | `citeproc: true` under `typst:` |
| A proper name lower-cased in a title, such as "Bank Marketing" | brace it in the `.bib`: `{Bank Marketing}` |
| The dataset's DOI is not in Crossref | it is a DataCite DOI: look it up there |
| In the PDF, the apostrophe of "ICML '05" curls the wrong way | leave abbreviated venue names out of the `.bib` |

## A check for every DOI {#sec-wp-check}

Opening every reference by hand is the first check; a script that repeats it before every
release is the second, and the one that survives a colleague adding an entry in a hurry:

::: {.prompt}
```default
Write scripts/check_refs.py: for every entry in references.bib with a DOI, look the record up (Crossref, or DataCite for a DataCite DOI) and fail if the DOI does not resolve or if the year, the first author's family name or the title disagree with the entry. Run it.
```
:::

The script needs the network, so it is a check you run before publishing, not part of the
render, which must work offline. Test it once on a deliberately broken copy of the `.bib`: a
wrong year, a changed title and a DOI that does not exist should each fail it. Here is one
entry of the project's `references.bib`, twice:

::: {#wp-spot .cell execution_count=3}
**A**

```bibtex
@article{moro2014datadriven,
  author  = {Moro, S{\'e}rgio and Cortez, Paulo and Rita, Paulo},
  title   = {A data-driven approach to predict the success of bank telemarketing},
  journal = {Decision Support Systems},
  volume  = {62},
  pages   = {22--31},
  year    = {2013},
  doi     = {10.1016/j.dss.2014.03.001}
}
```

**B**

```bibtex
@article{moro2014datadriven,
  author  = {Moro, S{\'e}rgio and Cortez, Paulo and Rita, Paulo},
  title   = {A data-driven approach to predict the success of bank telemarketing},
  journal = {Decision Support Systems},
  volume  = {62},
  pages   = {22--31},
  year    = {2014},
  doi     = {10.1016/j.dss.2014.03.001}
}
```

:::


::: think
One of A and B is the entry as published. What would `check_refs.py` report for the other,
and what would it not notice?

B is the entry as published. The script would fail A, with "moro2014datadriven: year 2013 in \.bib\, 2014 at Crossref": its DOI
is the same and resolves, but the year
disagrees with the registry's record. It would not notice that A's key still says
2014: a key is only a name, and the script compares the year, the first author and
the title.
:::

## A house template for the PDF {#sec-wp-template}

Quarto writes a Typst PDF from a template made of named parts, *template partials*, and you
can replace a part with your own. The one that styles the document is `typst-show.typ`; a
replacement can give the paper a title block with the company's logo and a label, a running
header and page numbers, in the brand's colours, which Quarto defines for it from
`_brand.yml`:

::: {.prompt .long}
```default
Give the PDF a house style: a Typst partial, templates/whitepaper/typst-show.typ, used from whitepaper.qmd's typst format with `template-partials`, that shows brand/logo.svg, the label "Technical white paper", the company and the date in a title block, and "page n of N" in the footer, in the brand's colours. Render the PDF and look at its first page.
```
:::

::: story
<!-- source: book/chapters/white-papers.qmd lines 201-203 at 651db10 ("a pattern written
"page 1 of 1" printed "pbge" on the second page") -->
The house template's page-number pattern was written `"page 1 of 1"`. On the second page
it printed "pbge". In a Typst pattern, letters are counters too: the "a" in "page" was read
as a request to count in letters, and the second page is "b". Keep words outside the
pattern, and look at a page that is not the first.
:::

Three more things to know about partials, in Quarto 1.10.20:

- **The company's name does not reach them.** Only the brand's colours, logo and typography
  do, so the finished paper names the company in a `company:` field of its own front matter.
- **A single-page render with `keep-typ` leaves files behind**, a `site_libs/` folder and the
  `.typ` source beside the sources: render the PDF with the whole site, or delete them.
- **Only Quarto's own partial names work** (`typst-show.typ`, `typst-template.typ`,
  `page.typ` and four more); any other name stops the render.

When a journal or a conference has its own format, use theirs instead of a house template:
Quarto's journal templates install with `quarto use template quarto-journals/<name>`, and the
venue's instructions come first.

::: catchup
```default
Catch me up: follow ../quarto-workshop/checkpoints/18-eval-whitepaper/README.md
```
:::

::: tryit
Write the paper, cite and check its references, and give the PDF the house template.

::: done
every cross-reference resolves in the PDF, the Word file and the web page; the three reference
lists match; `check_refs.py` reports no problems; and the PDF opens on the house title block.
:::
:::

## Summary {.unnumbered}

::: keyideas
- A white paper is read without you and checked by strangers: numbered sections,
  cross-referenced figures, tables and equations, and references that exist.
- Cross-references are labels (`sec-`, `tbl-`, `fig-`, `eq-`), and the render shows any that
  fail as "??".
- One CSL style file sets the citation style; `citeproc: true` makes a Typst PDF use it too.
- Cite only what you have opened, and let a script confirm every DOI before each release.
- A Typst template partial gives the PDF a house look from the brand; a journal's template
  replaces it when a venue has one.
:::

That completes the evaluation's set: a report, a model card, a deck, a site and a white paper,
all from one run of one script.
